text: NemoFleet: a robot fleet that learns from itself, built on Nebius Token Factory and NVIDIA Nemotron.

In a robot fleet, in a warehouse or a data center hall, every uncertain robot calls a large model in the cloud, even for problems another robot solved minutes ago. Ultra spends its time repeating answers instead of solving new ones.

Each robot runs Nemotron Nano as a fast reflex that returns an action and a confidence score. Robots also share precedents with the peers they pass, with no model call. If Nano is unsure, or the event is safety-critical, the gate escalates to Nemotron Ultra on Nebius Token Factory. Every output is validated against a typed schema, and a deterministic planner owns every trajectory, so paths are collision-free by construction.

The peer layer borrows two ideas from biology. A duck's leg runs warm and cold blood side by side in opposite directions, so heat transfers along its whole length. And ants on a trail swap information every time they pass.

When two robots pass, they swap a small, bounded payload: hazard precedents with their source, hop count, and time to live. Only the first robot to see a spill pays for a perception call. Everyone else learns it by handshake, and hazard tags on the map expire on their own.

A pairing scheduler adds pass-by waypoints, so a new robot meets peers only slightly ahead of it first. Each exchange stays small enough to absorb, and we test this against random pairing before claiming it.

Safety is never left to the model. A person in the lane always escalates to Ultra, whatever the peers say. Every model output is checked against a typed schema, and malformed actions are retried, never executed. And the planner, not the model, owns every trajectory.

Every night, NemoFleet runs one pipeline on Nebius. Replay: a Token Factory batch job has Ultra re-judge every decision Nano made that day, and flags the confident mistakes. Dream: Ultra writes counterfactual variants of the hardest episodes, and dozens of Serverless Jobs simulate them in parallel. Gate: each candidate lesson must fix its variants without regressing normal operations, so most are rejected. Consolidate: the survivors become a LoRA fine-tune of Nano on an H200 Serverless Job, tracked in MLflow. The new adapter is promoted on a vLLM endpoint only if it beats today's model.

The next morning, a different robot meets a variant it has never seen: a spill with a forklift at the same blind corner. It runs the promoted Nano, recognizes the situation with high confidence, and reroutes on its own. No call to Ultra.

The same fleet runs a second site. In a hyperscale data center hall, the hazard is a coolant leak at the end of a cold aisle, the person is a technician at a rack, and the Day 2 variant is the leak with a lift cart crossing. Only the scenario file changes. The gate, the peer layer, and Night Shift stay the same.

We measure all of it on Serverless Jobs: Ultra calls per hundred events, cost per task, latency, and success on held-out variants, for Nano only, Ultra only, the hybrid, and the hybrid with Night Shift. The edge lives it once. Nebius lives it hundreds of times.
